name: Context Budgeting
question: What earns a place in the window?
summary: Treat the context window as a scarce attention budget: fill it with the smallest set of high-signal tokens that gets the task done. Decide what enters, in what order and how much, because accuracy falls as input grows, even on simple tasks, and facts buried in the middle of a long prompt are the ones most often missed.
useCases: Agents that stuff whole documents, clause libraries or tool catalogues into every call
Quality that drops late in long sessions or on long inputs
Teams tempted to buy a bigger window instead of curating

items.detail: accuracy changes with input length even on simple tasks (Chroma, 18 models)
facts at the start or end are used best; the middle worst
in RULER only about half of models claiming 32k+ held up at 32k
long documents first, question last: up to 30% better in Anthropic’s tests
pass IDs and let tools fetch full text only when needed
accuracy at your real input lengths, per token spent

steps: Count tokens per segment: system prompt, documents, history, tool results
Find your effective budget: the length where your own eval stays accurate
Rank chunks by relevance and keep the top ones until the budget is spent
Put documents first and the question last; re-run the eval at 8k, 32k and 128k
pitfalls: Trusting the advertised maximum instead of measuring where accuracy falls
Leaving near-duplicate or outdated chunks in as distractors
Burying the most relevant chunk in the middle of a long prompt
remember: Fewer, better tokens. Key facts at the edges.
caption: Illustrative accuracies for one contract question. The pattern, not the exact numbers, is what the research shows.

steps.title: Inventory the window
steps.text: Count tokens per segment before sending. Here the clause library takes 90k of a 123k prompt; the system prompt, history and tools take the rest.

steps.title: Set an effective budget
steps.text: The advertised window is 200k, but your own eval stays accurate only up to about 16k on this task. That measured length is the budget.

steps.title: Rank by signal
steps.text: Score every chunk against the question and keep the top ones until the budget is spent. Five clauses, about 7.5k tokens, carry the answer.

steps.title: Order deliberately
steps.text: Documents go first, most relevant at the top, and the question goes last. Nothing critical sits in the middle of a long block.

steps.title: Load just in time
steps.text: Instead of full text for all 60 clauses, pass a short index of IDs and titles, and a get_clause tool the agent calls when it needs one.

steps.title: Re-test at length
steps.text: Run the same eval with inputs padded to 8k, 32k and 128k. The drop at 128k is why the budget exists; re-check it when models change.

pros: Raises accuracy on long inputs, often more than a bigger model would
Cuts cost and latency along with tokens
Needs no new infrastructure: counting, ranking and ordering
Makes failures easier to debug: you know what the model saw
cons: Needs a length eval to find the effective budget
A chunk cut in error can remove the one fact that mattered
Relevance scores depend on your retriever or re-ranker
Budgets must be re-measured when models change
avoidWhen: Inputs are already short and fixed (little to curate)
The task genuinely needs the whole document at once, such as a full-text diff

playgroundGuide.scenario: A contract-review agent answers “Can the buyer terminate for delay?” from a supply agreement split into 40 clauses of 3k tokens, ranked by relevance. The answer needs the clauses ranked 1, 2 and 4. You decide how much goes into the prompt, whether outdated near-duplicate clauses sneak in, where the key clause sits and whether the question comes last. Accuracy follows a fixed, illustrative curve shaped like the published findings.
controls: Drag the context size to set how many ranked chunks fit, from 4k to 200k tokens.
Add near-duplicate distractors: outdated clause versions that take space and confuse the model.
Move the key fact to the start, middle or end, and toggle documents-first, question-last.

presets.name: Starting prompt
presets.expect: 128k tokens: 38 relevant chunks and 4 distractors, key clause in the middle, question first. All 3 facts, but accuracy is only 48% at $0.384 a call.

presets.name: Use the whole window
presets.expect: 200k allowed, 140k sent with 6 distractors: accuracy falls to 42%. More room did not help.

presets.name: Curated to 16k
presets.expect: 14k tokens, 4 chunks, no distractors: accuracy 84%, 89% fewer tokens, even with the key clause in the middle.

presets.name: 32k, key fact buried
presets.expect: 32k tokens with the question last, but the key clause in the middle: 73%.

missions.text: Reach at least 85% accuracy with all 3 required facts included.
missions.hint: Try 16k with no distractors, the key fact at the start and the question last.

missions.text: Cut tokens by at least 70% from the start without losing accuracy.
missions.hint: 70% fewer than 128k means 38k or less; 16k or 32k with no distractors both work.

missions.text: Gain at least 10 points just by moving the key fact out of the middle.
missions.hint: The middle penalty grows with length and is largest from about 32k. Compare middle with start at 32k.

practice.scenario: A contract-review agent at a Mumbai law firm loaded all 60 clauses of a supply agreement for every question, about 90,000 tokens. Answers to “Can the buyer terminate for delay?” kept missing an exception buried in clause 31. The team now counts tokens per segment, ranks clauses against the question, keeps the top 5 (about 7,000 tokens), puts them first and the question last, and re-runs its 50-question eval at each input length.

industries.use: Send the few clauses that bear on the question, not the whole agreement
Load the two relevant circulars and the client’s last orders, not the full rulebook
Put the policy wording and the claim form first, the adjuster’s question last

practice.analogy: A barrister’s brief to the judge. The judge could read the whole case file, but the brief puts the three decisive documents on top and the question at the end.

library.name: Anthropic SDK (token counting)
library.what: messages.count_tokens returns the input token count for a request before you send it, so you can budget each segment.

practice.note: score each clause with your retriever or re-ranker; count_tokens is a free endpoint with its own rate limits, so cache counts for fixed clauses.

samples.code:
import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
MODEL = "claude-sonnet-4-5"          # use your current model
BUDGET = 8_000                       # effective budget found by your own length eval

def tokens(text: str) -> int:
    r = client.messages.count_tokens(model=MODEL,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": text}])
    return r.input_tokens

def build_prompt(question: str, clauses: list[tuple[float, str]]) -> str:
    kept, used = [], tokens(question)
    for score, text in sorted(clauses, reverse=True):     # highest relevance first
        t = tokens(text)
        if used + t > BUDGET:
            break
        kept.append(text); used += t
    docs = "\n".join(f"<clause>{c}</clause>" for c in kept)
    return f"{docs}\n\nQuestion: {question}"               # documents first, query last

numericDrill.question: An agent sends 60 clauses of 1,500 tokens each plus a 500-token question on every call. You keep the top 5 clauses instead. By what percentage do input tokens fall?

interview.question: Why not just use the model with the biggest context window?
interview.answer: Advertised length is not effective length: accuracy falls as input grows even on simple tasks, distractors hurt more at long lengths, and facts in the middle are used worst. A bigger window also costs more per call. Curate first, then measure accuracy at your real lengths.

interview.question: How do you choose what goes into the window?
interview.answer: Inventory tokens per segment, rank candidate chunks by relevance, keep the top ones until an effective budget found by your own eval, place documents first and the question last, and load everything else just in time through tools.

mistakes.mistake: Sizing the prompt to the advertised maximum
mistakes.fix: Measure where your own eval accuracy drops and budget below it

mistakes.mistake: Placing the key chunk in the middle of a long prompt
mistakes.fix: Put the most relevant material at the start and the question at the end

quiz.question: A contract-review agent sends all 60 clauses (90k tokens) with every question and keeps missing an exception in clause 31. What is the first change?
options: Switch to a model with a 1M-token window
Rank clauses against the question and send only the top few
Repeat the question at the start of the prompt
Raise the temperature so the model explores more
quiz.explanation: Curating to the few relevant clauses removes distractors and shortens the input, which is what restores accuracy.

quiz.question: A claims agent receives 40 policy chunks of 2,500 tokens and a 500-token question. You keep the top 6 chunks. How many input tokens remain?
Which findings support curating context rather than filling a large window? Select all that apply.
options: Accuracy changes with input length even on simple tasks
Facts in the middle of long inputs are used worst
Every model performs equally well up to its advertised maximum
Longer prompts always cost less per useful answer
quiz.explanation: Context-rot and lost-in-the-middle results both favour curating. Advertised length is often not effective length, and longer prompts cost more.

quiz.question: A loan-policy assistant scores 92% on questions at 8k tokens and 71% when the same questions are padded to 128k. What should the context budget be based on?
options: The advertised 200k window
The length where your own eval stays accurate
The average document length
Whatever fits after the system prompt
quiz.explanation: The budget is the measured effective length for your task, not the model’s advertised maximum.

quiz.question: A clinical-guideline assistant places the key dosage table in the middle of a 60k-token prompt. Accuracy is poor. What is the cheapest fix?
options: Move the most relevant material to the start and put the question last
Add a second copy of the whole guideline
Switch to a larger model
Lower max_tokens
quiz.explanation: Models use information at the start and end best; the middle is the weakest position.

quiz.question: Your prompt costs $3 per million input tokens. Cutting a 120,000-token prompt to 12,000 tokens saves how much per 1,000 calls?
quiz.explanation: Saving per call: 108,000 × $3/M = $0.324. Over 1,000 calls: $324.

quiz.question: A plan-comparison agent loads 80 tariff sheets per question. Which changes follow context-budgeting practice? Select all that apply.
options: Pass a short index of tariff IDs and a tool to fetch one sheet
Put the customer’s question after the retrieved sheets
Add outdated tariff versions so the model sees the history
Pad the prompt to the model’s maximum for consistency
quiz.explanation: Just-in-time loading and query-last ordering both follow the practice. Outdated versions are distractors; padding adds rot.

quiz.question: RULER tested 17 models that all claimed at least 32k context. About how many performed satisfactorily at 32k?
options: All 17
About half
Only one
None
quiz.explanation: RULER found only about half held up at 32k, showing that claimed length is not effective length.

quiz.question: A support agent’s prompt has a 3k system prompt, 40k of help articles, 22k of history and 15k of tool results. What share of the 80k prompt is help articles?
Two near-duplicate versions of a termination clause (2019 and 2024) are both in the prompt. What is the risk?
options: None: more context is always safer
The outdated clause acts as a distractor and can be quoted as current
The model will refuse to answer
The prompt cache will be disabled
quiz.explanation: Near-duplicate distractors hurt more as inputs grow; the model may cite the outdated version.

quiz.question: Which belong in a context-budgeting pipeline for a dispute-resolution agent? Select all that apply.
options: Token counts per segment before sending
A relevance score for each candidate chunk
An eval run at several input lengths
Random shuffling of chunk order on each call
quiz.explanation: Counting, ranking and testing at length are the core steps. Random order puts key facts in the middle at random.

quiz.question: Anthropic’s long-context guidance says to put long documents before the query. In its tests, up to how much did this improve response quality?
options: It made no difference
quiz.explanation: The guidance reports up to 30% better quality with the query at the end.

quiz.question: A tutor agent has an effective budget of 16k. The question takes 500 tokens and each notes chunk is 1,500 tokens. How many chunks fit?
A route-planning agent performs well at 20k but badly at 150k, even though all needed facts are present at 150k. What explains this?
options: The model cannot read more than 20k tokens
Context rot: accuracy falls as input length grows
The prompt cache expired
Tool calls failed at 150k
quiz.explanation: All facts can be present and accuracy can still fall as the input grows.

quiz.question: A compliance assistant must answer from 3 circulars among 200. Which prompt designs are sound? Select all that apply.
options: Top 3 circulars first, question last
An index of all 200 circular titles, with a fetch tool
All 200 circulars, with the 3 relevant ones in the middle
All 200 circulars repeated twice for emphasis
quiz.explanation: Curated top chunks and just-in-time loading both work. Burying or repeating everything adds rot and cost.

quiz.question: Your prompt builder puts the highest-scoring chunk in the centre “for balance”. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: balance helps attention
It places the best chunk where models use information worst
It makes the prompt longer
It breaks token counting
quiz.explanation: The centre of a long prompt is the lost-in-the-middle zone; the best chunk belongs at the start.

quiz.question: Which tool counts input tokens for a Claude request before you send it?
options: The messages.count_tokens endpoint
tiktoken
The Batch API
RULER
quiz.explanation: Claude’s token-counting endpoint returns input_tokens for a request; tiktoken is for OpenAI tokenizers.

quiz.question: Accuracy is 88% at 8k, 84% at 32k and 62% at 128k. Your prompts average 90k. What do you do?
options: Nothing: 90k is below the 200k window
Curate prompts down to about 32k or less
Increase to 128k to be safe
Add more examples to the prompt
quiz.explanation: The eval shows accuracy holding to about 32k and falling sharply after, so curate below that.

quiz.question: A context budget of 12k must hold a 1,000-token system prompt, a 400-token question and chunks of 2,200 tokens. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: 4 chunks fit
5 chunks fit
The 4 chunks plus overhead total 10,200 tokens
The 5 chunks plus overhead total 12,400 tokens, over budget

quiz.question: A team wants to skip curation because “the model has a huge window”. What single piece of evidence settles it?
options: The model’s marketing page
Your own eval run at your real input lengths
A public scoreboard ranking
The average prompt length last month
quiz.explanation: Only your own eval at your lengths shows whether accuracy holds.
